metadata.title: How Technology Changes Demands for Human Skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper is conceptual and does not analyze a student-level ILSA micro-dataset. It discusses how PIAAC frameworks would measure foundational and advanced skills (numeracy, literacy/reading, and problem-solving in technology-rich environments) and how these constructs relate to technology-driven changes in work. Because no analytic sample is constructed from PIAAC microdata, there is no application of complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures. The appropriate weighting guidance for PIAAC would depend on the PIAAC technical documentation, but this paper itself does not perform weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not conduct an empirical analysis predicting or estimating cognitive achievement outcomes from PIAAC microdata; it is a framework/argument paper about what PIAAC should measure. As a result, plausible values (PV-based achievement scores) and any missing-data handling strategy are not part of the study’s methodology. The absence of PV/missing-data reporting reflects the paper’s non-empirical nature rather than a transparency gap in an ML estimation pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level dataset is analyzed. The paper provides a conceptual mapping between technology-driven workplace task demands and the skill domains assessed in PIAAC (numeracy, literacy/reading, and problem-solving in technology-rich environments), plus an additional communication construct not tested in the current PIAAC version.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper is not an empirical large-scale assessment study; it is a conceptual argument that situates PIAAC-measured competencies within technology-driven changes in work. It proposes that a technology-rich workplace requires foundational skills (numeracy and literacy/reading) and an advanced problem-solving skill (Expert Thinking, aligned with PIAAC’s Problem Solving in Technology-Rich Environments), while also identifying an advanced communication skill (Complex Communication) that is not currently tested in PIAAC. The paper describes the breadth of the PIAAC frameworks for literacy, numeracy, and technology-rich problem solving, including the role of digital tools and metacognition in problem solving. It also frames PIAAC as an “early warning system” for countries’ preparedness for rapid technical change, while noting limitations of the current PIAAC version regarding Complex Communication and certain numeracy aspects. No model performance metrics, sampling design, or PV/missing-data procedures are reported because no ML or statistical estimation is conducted.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction contains many nulls because the document is a non-empirical OECD working paper that develops and motivates assessment frameworks rather than analyzing ILSA microdata. There is no analytic sample, no country-level breakdown, and no ML model training/evaluation; therefore fields such as total_students, countries, PV handling, missing-data handling, and main_findings are not applicable to an estimation pipeline. The paper’s contribution is policy-relevant conceptual guidance on which skills PIAAC should measure to reflect technology-driven workplace demands.
